The yellow perch Perca flavescens displays a maximum recorded total length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm] in its northern range, though individuals in southern populations rarely exceed 40 cm. This species attains sexual maturity upon reaching a total length of 19.2 cm [Lp = 19.2 cm], a benchmark that typically corresponds to the transition from juvenile foraging strategies to reproductive allocation. Field surveys conducted in Lake Erie indicate that females at this length have completed vitellogenesis and are capable of spawning. The relationship between length and mass follows the equation 0.01230 times total length raised to the 3.04 power, which produces an estimated ultimate wet weight of 1,800 grams [Wwi = 1,800 grams] for a 50 cm individual. This asymptotic mass represents the maximum body size achievable under optimal growing conditions, and it is rarely observed in exploited populations where size-selective mortality truncates the age structure. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this length-weight scaling is conservative within the genus Perca, with minor deviations attributable to differences in body depth and condition factor across habitats.

At the onset of reproductive maturity, the typical wet weight at puberty is 98 grams [Wwp = 98 grams], as derived from the length-weight relationship applied to the 19.2 cm [Lp = 19.2 cm] total length at puberty. This mass threshold is substantially lower than the ultimate wet weight of 1,800 grams [Wwi = 1,800 grams], indicating that yellow perch channel considerable somatic growth into post-maturation body size increases. The eggs themselves, which are demersal and adhesive, exhibit a diameter of approximately 2.25 mm based on observations in the closely related Perca fluviatilis. From this egg diameter, the estimated wet weight at birth for a newly fertilized ovum is 0.006 grams [Wwb = 0.006 grams], a value that reflects the modest yolk reserves allocated to the endotrophic larval phase. This initial mass is several orders of magnitude smaller than the mass at puberty, underscoring the pronounced ontogenetic increase in body size that characterizes this iteroparous percid. Yolk-dependent embryos rely entirely on endogenous nutrients until the onset of exogenous feeding, at which point the trophic switch to zooplankton consumption begins.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the maximum daily reproduction rate of Perca flavescens reaches approximately 168 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 168 eggs per day]. Females produce approximately 168 eggs per clutch during a single spawning event, a relatively modest fecundity for a percid of this body size, and they typically engage in one spawning event per year, although some southern populations may exhibit a second, smaller spawning pulse during extended warm seasons. This reproductive allocation pattern reflects the trade-off between egg size and fecundity, where larger eggs improve early larval survival at the expense of total offspring number.

Maximum longevity in Perca flavescens has been documented at 11 years [am = 11 years] under natural conditions, a duration that corresponds to approximately 4,015 days when individuals experience the thermal regime typical of temperate lakes at 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This value is derived from scale annulus readings and otolith-based age validation studies conducted across the species' range, which consistently indicate that senescence becomes evident after the eighth year. The cool-water thermal optimum appears to slow the accumulation of physiological damage, allowing some individuals to persist for over a decade. By contrast, populations inhabiting warmer southern reservoirs where summer temperatures routinely exceed 25 °C rarely produce individuals older than six years, suggesting that elevated metabolic costs accelerate the rate of aging. The documented lifespan of 11 years [am = 11 years] at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] positions Perca flavescens as a moderately long-lived percid, intermediate between the shorter-lived darters and the more long-lived walleye Sander vitreus, which can exceed 20 years in cold, oligotrophic lakes.

The early life stages of Perca flavescens are characterized by rapid growth following the transition from lecithotrophic dependence to exogenous feeding. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae weigh just 0.006 grams [Wwb = 0.006 grams] at the moment of chorion rupture, a mass that is comparable to that of other temperate percids with similar egg diameters. By the time these larvae reach the juvenile stage and recruit to benthic habitats, they typically achieve the wet weight at puberty of 98 grams [Wwp = 98 grams] within two to three growing seasons under favorable conditions. An individual that reaches the ultimate wet weight of 1,800 grams [Wwi = 1,800 grams] would therefore have increased its body mass by a factor of 300,000 relative to its hatchling size, a remarkable ontogenetic trajectory that reflects the high productivity of their preferred lacustrine environments. Age validation studies using marked recaptures confirm that the growth rate is highly plastic and modulated by prey availability, with faster growth documented in populations exploiting abundant zebra mussel druses that support dense benthic invertebrate communities.
